Task and constraints: A valid IP address consists of exactly four integers separated by single dots. Each integer is between 0 and 255 (inclusive) and cannot have leading zeros. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Tries candidate segment lengths for four address components, rejects segments with invalid ranges or leading zeroes, and joins valid quadruples.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking explores the bounded segment choices required for an IPv4 address.
Invariant: The partial path contains valid segments and the unconsumed suffix must fit into the remaining segment slots.
Edge cases: Leading-zero segments such as '00' are invalid; each segment has at most three digits. The code enumerates only four parts.
Complexity: The author labels a constant-depth O(3^4) search with O(n*m) space; output storage can dominate when many addresses are valid.

Task and constraints: Given an integer n, return the number of structurally unique BST's (binary search trees) which has exactly n nodes of unique values from 1 to n. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Uses the Catalan recurrence: for each possible root, multiplies the number of left and right BST shapes and sums those products; memoization or recursion is used as shown in the code.
Technique and why it applies: Counting BST shapes by root choice decomposes each tree into independent left and right subtrees.
Invariant: For each n, the result sums all left-size/right-size combinations whose sizes add to n-1.
Edge cases: n=0 and n=1 are base cases. Without memoization, repeated recursive subproblems cause substantial repeated work.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Memoized DP is O(n^2) time and O(n) space; a plain recursive version can be exponential.

Task and constraints: Given strings s1, s2, and s3, find whether s3 is formed by an interleaving of s1 and s2. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Fills a boolean table over prefixes of s1 and s2; a cell is true if the next character of s3 can come from either source prefix whose last character matches.
Technique and why it applies: Two-dimensional DP combines the two possible sources of the next character.
Invariant: dp[i][j] describes whether the first i characters of s1 and j of s2 form the first i+j characters of s3.
Edge cases: Unequal total lengths fail immediately; empty prefixes rely on the table's initial row and column.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and space when a full table is used, matching all prefix pairs.

Task and constraints: Given strings s1, s2, and s3, find whether s3 is formed by an interleaving of s1 and s2. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Uses a one-dimensional DP row to determine whether prefixes can interleave, updating in place from the prior row and current row's left state.
Technique and why it applies: Rolling-row DP keeps only the previous/current prefix states.
Invariant: Each cell describes whether the combined source prefixes match the corresponding output prefix.
Edge cases: Unequal total lengths fail immediately; update order matters because left state is already from the current row.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and O(m+n) space; the active DP storage is one dimension, so the label may overstate auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Given strings s1, s2, and s3, find whether s3 is formed by an interleaving of s1 and s2. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Recursively tests whether prefixes of s1 and s2 can form the prefix of s3, memoizing index states. A transition consumes the next matching character from either source string.
Technique and why it applies: Memoized recursion explores the two legal ways to form the next output character.
Invariant: A state (i,j) asks whether s3's first i+j characters can be formed from the first i and j characters of the source strings.
Edge cases: Different total lengths fail immediately; equal characters in both source strings may create two branches, which memoization avoids repeating.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and space, consistent with index-pair states and memoization, plus recursion depth O(m+n).

Task and constraints: Given two strings s and t, return the number of distinct subsequences of s which equals t. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Recursively or iteratively counts ways to form target as a subsequence of source, branching on whether a matching source character is used or skipped.
Technique and why it applies: Subsequence DP/backtracking fits because each source character may be skipped or matched to the next target character.
Invariant: The current state tracks the source and target positions already consumed.
Edge cases: If target is longer than source, there are no matches; repeated characters create multiple distinct index choices.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Memoized DP is O(|s|*|t|) time/space; plain recursion can be exponential, depending on the code's caching.

Task and constraints: Given two strings s and t, return the number of distinct subsequences of s which equals t. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Initializes ways[0]=1 and scans source characters backward through target positions. Matching characters add ways for the target prefix with that character removed.
Technique and why it applies: One-dimensional subsequence DP counts distinct ways to match target prefixes without reusing a source character.
Invariant: ways[j] counts matches for the first j target characters using the source prefix processed so far; reverse update order preserves the previous source prefix.
Edge cases: An empty target has one match; a target longer than source has zero. Counts can grow large.
Complexity: The author labels O(n^2) time and O(n) space; more precisely time is O(|s|*|t|) and space O(|t|).

Task and constraints: Given a binary tree The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Traverses each tree level and connects nodes to their next neighbor using queue or existing next links as shown by the implementation; it returns the root.
Technique and why it applies: Level-order traversal can identify neighboring nodes at the same depth.
Invariant: Each node's next pointer is set to the next node on its level, or left null at the level end.
Edge cases: An empty root returns null; the final node at each level must not retain a stale next pointer.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n); auxiliary space depends on implementation, typically O(width) for a queue or O(1) for a next-pointer traversal.

Task and constraints: Given an integer numRows, return the first numRows of Pascal's triangle. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Starts with the first row [1], then builds each following row with 1 at both ends and sums adjacent entries from the previous row for interior positions.
Technique and why it applies: Pascal's triangle recurrence builds each coefficient from the two above it.
Invariant: Each row contains binomial coefficients for its row index and has ones at both ends.
Edge cases: One row returns [[1]]; zero rows returns [] if guarded. The output stores all generated rows.
Complexity: The author labels O(n^2) time and O(1) space when present, but storing the triangle requires O(n^2) output space.

Task and constraints: Given an integer rowIndex, return the rowIndex^th (0-indexed) row of the Pascal's triangle. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Builds the requested Pascal row by updating coefficients in place from right to left so each value uses the prior row's values.
Technique and why it applies: In-place Pascal recurrence computes a row without storing all earlier rows.
Invariant: Before an update, entries to the left still represent the previous iteration, so reverse order prevents overwriting needed values.
Edge cases: rowIndex=0 returns [1]; reverse update order is essential to avoid reusing a newly updated coefficient.
Complexity: The author labels O(n^2) time and O(1) space for in-place storage; the returned row itself requires O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Given a triangle array, return the minimum path sum from top to bottom. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Maintains minimum path sums by comparing the two adjacent positions in the next row and adding the current value.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming exploits the two downward choices in a triangle.
Invariant: The current value stores the best total through the position considered so far.
Edge cases: A one-row triangle returns its value; the code assumes nonempty input.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(total triangle cells), O(n^2) for n rows; auxiliary space depends on whether the implementation copies rows.

Task and constraints: Given a triangle array, return the minimum path sum from top to bottom. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Uses a rolling array of costs from the bottom of the triangle upward, replacing each entry by its value plus the smaller of its two children.
Technique and why it applies: Bottom-up DP combines the two possible next-row choices.
Invariant: Each stored value is the minimum path sum from that triangle position to the bottom for the rows already processed.
Edge cases: A one-row triangle returns its sole value; the triangle is assumed nonempty.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and O(n) space; each triangle entry is processed once and only a row-sized array is needed.

Task and constraints: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i^th day. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Tracks the minimum price seen so far and the best profit from selling at the current price; returns the best single-transaction profit.
Technique and why it applies: A running minimum avoids checking every buy/sell pair.
Invariant: min_price is the lowest earlier/current price and max_profit is the best difference seen.
Edge cases: Decreasing prices return zero; an empty list is handled only if the code has a guard.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space when present; one pass and scalar state support those bounds.

Task and constraints: You are given an integer array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i^th day. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Tracks whether it is waiting for a valley or holding an open rising run. It subtracts a local minimum when an upslope begins, adds a local peak when the upslope ends, and adds the final price if still on a rise.
Technique and why it applies: Valley/peak detection sums gains over increasing runs.
Invariant: ans accumulates buy costs negatively and sale prices positively for completed rises.
Edge cases: A strictly decreasing sequence makes no trades; a final increasing run is sold at the last price. Empty input may fail at prices[-1] if state remains hill.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n), auxiliary space O(1).

Task and constraints: You are given an integer array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i^th day. The method returns the requested value or collection.
Idea: Adds every positive adjacent price difference, which equals the profit from collecting all upward movements.
Technique and why it applies: Greedy summation is valid when multiple transactions are allowed and there is no transaction penalty.
Invariant: profit is the sum of positive gains between consecutive days.
Edge cases: Decreasing/equal days add zero; an empty or one-day list returns zero.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space, consistent with a single pass.
